title: Why training fades, and how to make it stick

narration: A quick question about your last training.
How much could you still explain today?
beats.visual_intent: the presenter greets the viewer beside the lesson title

narration: On Monday, she leaves a great workshop,
By Wednesday, one has gone fuzzy.
By Friday, most of it has gone quiet.
beats.visual_intent: Maya at her desk with three bright ideas in a thought bubble; across the week the ideas grey out and drift away one by one

grounding.claim: Maya and her week are an invented illustration
forgetting is fastest soon after learning

narration: you will have a simple way to beat it.
on_screen: and how to make it stick
beats.visual_intent: the lesson title prints large; a promise line settles under it
a recall bar full on the training day drains toward empty a week later

grounding.claim: recall falls in the days after learning (shape only, no numbers)

narration: He learned lists of nonsense syllables,
then tested what he kept over time.
beats.visual_intent: a notebook of syllable cards; he learns them, then tests himself later and some cards flip to blank

grounding.claim: Ebbinghaus measured his own memory with nonsense syllables and published in 1885

narration: What he found has a name,
How steep depends on you and the material.
beats.visual_intent: axes of recall over time; the curve draws itself, steep then flat; faint alternative curves show it varies by person

grounding.claim: the forgetting curve drops steeply then levels off
the rate varies; no single percentage

recall.prompt: where does most of the forgetting happen?

narration: So, where does most of the forgetting happen?
beats.visual_intent: one short line, large, as a thing to hold on to

grounding.claim: forgetting is fastest soon after learning

beats.visual_intent: Maya at her laptop, eyes on her notes; the lines of the notes highlight one after another

grounding.claim: an invented illustration of a common habit

beats.visual_intent: a familiarity gauge climbs high as she rereads, looking reassuring

grounding.claim: rereading feels effective because the material becomes familiar

narration: But familiar is not the same
as being able to recall it.
beats.visual_intent: the notes page is covered; the thought bubble tries to pull the lines back and finds only question marks

grounding.claim: familiarity is mistaken for being able to recall

narration: and pull the ideas back out.
beats.visual_intent: Maya thinks hard; the three ideas come back into her bubble one by one; the name arrives last

grounding.claim: retrieval practice means actively recalling information

beats.visual_intent: two columns as equals, rereading against testing, each claim arriving as it is said

grounding.claim: retrieval practice beats rereading for long-term retention
rereading feels easy because it is familiar

narration: A self-test takes a few minutes.
Then check it against the notes.
The check is part of the learning.
beats.visual_intent: three steps, each arriving as it is spoken, the check marked as part of the learning

grounding.claim: a few minutes of recall then checking counts
checking provides feedback that matters

narration: and the next drop is slower.
beats.visual_intent: the forgetting curve returns; at each test it jumps back up and the next drop is gentler, a staircase of flatter curves

grounding.claim: each successful recall makes the memory more durable

narration: and it lasts longer than cramming it together.
beats.visual_intent: the term, its one-line definition, and a concrete workplace example

grounding.claim: spaced practice beats massed practice for long-term retention

beats.misconception: one long review is as good as several short ones
narration: What about one long review on Friday?
beats.visual_intent: a cramming gauge shoots up for tomorrow, then drains faster than you expect

grounding.claim: cramming helps shortly afterwards but fades faster

recall.question: Same training, two plans. Which keeps more after a month?

narration: Plan A, one long review on Friday.
Plan B, three short self-tests, spread out.
Which keeps more after a month?
on_screen: Which keeps more after a month?
beats.visual_intent: the question and two options as peers, then a real pause with a countdown

grounding.claim: the quiz contrasts massed and spaced practice

narration: Spaced self-tests keep more, for longer.
but it is one long reread,
beats.visual_intent: the right option is marked; the explanation, then why the tempting option loses

grounding.claim: spaced retrieval beats massed rereading
massed study fades faster

narration: Here is the plan for your next training.
The second, a few days later.
The third, a week or two after that.
beats.visual_intent: Maya travels a path across the calendar, stopping at each test as it is named

grounding.claim: a practical guideline: about a day, a few days, a week or two

narration: It is a guideline, not a rule.
If a test feels easy, stretch the next gap.
If it feels hard, bring it closer.
beats.visual_intent: two peer cards: the easy case and the hard case

grounding.claim: stretch gaps when recall is easy, shorten when it fails
later reviews can come after longer gaps

narration: And put all three in your calendar,
beats.visual_intent: a calendar page; three self-test entries drop onto their days and tick

grounding.claim: applying the guideline schedule

narration: Weeks later, she still has it.
beats.visual_intent: Maya again, happy; the three ideas return and this time they stay bright

grounding.claim: Maya is an invented illustration
spaced retrieval supports long-term retention

narration: Test it, space it, test it again.
on_screen: Test it. Space it. Test it again.
beats.visual_intent: three tokens light up in turn, joined by a thread; the pocket rule stamps last

grounding.claim: summary of F2, F4, F6

narration: Your next training starts the clock.
and more of it will stick.
beats.visual_intent: the presenter closes, warm, beside the pocket rule

grounding.claim: spaced retrieval improves retention
